504	=== hdr10-peak.mdx
505	---
506	title: "HDR10 peak"
507	description: "See the peak brightness Frame Job read from a PQ file, override it when the metadata is wrong or missing, and go back to the file's own value."
508	---
509	
510	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
511	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
512	
513	HDR10 video uses the PQ transfer curve, so Frame Job calls it a PQ file. Such a file's metadata names how bright its highlights get, and Frame Job eases them down to white at that brightness, its peak, rather than cutting them off flat. The peak is read when you import the file, and the **HDR10** section lets you see it and change it when the metadata is wrong or missing.
514	
515	<AtAGlance
516	  where="Media tab ▸ HDR10"
517	  tools={['set_media_color', 'get_project']}
518	/>
519	
520	## The peak a file names
521	
522	Import reads the peak by itself, so most files need nothing from you. It takes MaxCLL, the brightest pixel the file says it holds, when that's present and not zero. Otherwise it takes the maximum of the display the file was mastered on.
523	
524	| The file is | Frame Job looks in |
525	| --- | --- |
526	| A video | The description stored with the video track. When that carries no HDR10 metadata at all, the video stream's own (HEVC SEI or AV1 metadata), so files from ffmpeg, HandBrake or x265 are read too. |
527	| A PNG still | Its `cLLI` and `mDCV` chunks. |
528	| A HEIF or HEIC still | The `clli` and `mdcv` boxes of its main image. |
529	
530	A file that names no peak is still read as PQ, and it's treated as 1,000 cd/m².
531	
532	What the peak does depends on the [project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/):
533	
534	- **In an SDR project**, highlights roll off smoothly to white at the peak. A peak below 203 cd/m², HDR reference white (the level ordinary white sits at), counts as 203.
535	- **In an HDR (HLG) project**, the picture keeps display light up to 1,000 cd/m². A peak above that rolls brighter highlights off to fit, and a lower peak doesn't change the picture.
536	
537	## The HDR10 section
538	
539	The **HDR10** section of the **Media** tab appears once the project has a PQ file, either a video or a still.
540	
541	Click the file in the list to see and change its peak. The section's header shows the selected file's peak, for example "4,000 cd/m²", so you can read it with the section collapsed.
542	
543	When the selected row isn't a PQ file, the section reads "Select a PQ file in the list" and its controls are disabled.
544	
545	## Set a peak by hand
546	
547	Override the file's peak when its metadata is wrong, or when it has none and you know the real figure.
548	
549	<Steps>
550	
551	1. On the **Media** tab, click the PQ file in the list.
552	
553	2. In the **HDR10** section, type a value in **Peak** and press <kbd>↩</kbd>, or click the chevron for a [quick pick](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#use-a-quick-pick).
554	
555	</Steps>
556	
557	**Peak** takes whole numbers from 1 to 10,000 cd/m², and its quick picks are 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 10,000. A typed number outside the range is held to the nearest end. Entering the value already showing isn't a new choice, so it makes no undo step.
558	
559	## Use File's
560	
561	**Use File's** clears your override and goes back to the peak the file's HDR10 metadata names. A file with no metadata goes back to the assumed 1,000 cd/m².
562	
563	The button is available only while an override is set.
564	
565	## Where the peak came from
566	
567	A line under the controls says where the peak came from.
568	
569	| The line says | What it means |
570	| --- | --- |
571	| "Mastered at 4,000 cd/m² (MaxCLL, from the file)" | The file's own value. |
572	| "No HDR10 metadata — 1,000 cd/m² assumed" | The file names no peak. |
573	| "Set by hand; the file says 1,000 cd/m² (mastering display)" | Your override, with the value it replaces. |
574	| "Set by hand; the file has no HDR10 metadata" | Your override, on a file with no metadata. |
575	
576	## Undo and Camera Log
577	
578	Each change is one undo step, **PQ Peak**.
579	
580	The peak and the [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) keep each other. Changing the peak keeps the file's Camera Log setting, and changing the Camera Log, even to **None**, keeps the peak.
581	
582	## Good to know
583	
584	- The peak belongs to the media file, not to a clip, so two clips of one file can't be read differently.
585	- Only a PQ file has a peak, so the section's controls are disabled for anything else.
586	- The peak is read once, at import. Relinking a PQ file doesn't read it again, so set it by hand if the new file differs. A file that wasn't PQ when you imported it can't take a peak after you relink it to one.
587	- A PQ still takes a peak and nothing else. Camera Log is for video files.
588	- The peak describes a source file. An [HDR10 export](/hdr/export-hdr/) carries fixed metadata of its own, whatever the peak is.
589	
590	## With an agent
591	
592	`set_media_color` sets a PQ file's peak with `peak` in its `color`, a whole number of cd/m². A PQ still takes `peak` alone. `get_project` shows the file's own reading in `media[].color.pq`, where an empty `{}` means the file names no peak.
593	
594	Two things differ from the app:
595	
596	- The call replaces the Camera Log and the peak together, so an agent that wants to keep both sends both. In the app each control keeps the other.
597	- `color: null` clears the Camera Log and a peak override together, and the peak goes back to the file's own reading.
598	
599	The call fails in two cases where the app can't go wrong:
600	
601	| The agent sends | What comes back |
602	| --- | --- |
603	| A peak outside 1 to 10,000, which the field would hold to the range | "color.peak must be 1–10000 cd/m², not …" |
604	| A peak on a file that isn't PQ | "media N is not a PQ file; only a PQ file takes a peak" |
605	
606	See [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/).
607	
608	## Related
609	
610	- [How sources are read](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/)
611	- [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/)
612	- [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/)
613	- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)
614	=== how-sources-are-read.mdx
615	---
616	title: How sources are read
617	description: How Frame Job reads each kind of video and photo you bring in, and what it converts in an SDR project and in an HDR (HLG) project.
618	---
619	
620	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
621	
622	Frame Job reads each source as what it is: ordinary video, HLG video, an HDR10 file, wide-gamut footage or camera log. You don't need to set anything for most footage, because the file's own colour labels say how to read it. The one kind you may have to name yourself is camera log.
623	
624	<AtAGlance
625	  menu={['File ▸ Add Media…', 'View ▸ Show Ungraded']}
626	  keys={['⇧⌘I', '⌃⌘U']}
627	  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log', 'Media tab ▸ HDR10']}
628	  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color']}
629	/>
630	
631	## One conversion at the start
632	
633	Each frame of a source is converted once, before anything else happens to it, into the colour the project works in. That's Rec. 709 in an SDR project and Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 in an HDR (HLG) project. See [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/) for how to choose.
634	
635	The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture, so they work the same whatever the file was. The file's labels choose the conversion, and a [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) set on the file chooses before its labels. The conversion is Frame Job's own, for HLG, PQ and wide-gamut sources alike.
636	
637	An SDR project that holds only Rec. 709 sources isn't converted at all. Its pixels and labels stay exactly as they are, because Frame Job turns the conversion on only when a source needs it.
638	
639	A few terms come up below. A file's **primaries** say which colours its red, green and blue are, and its **transfer curve** says how its numbers turn into brightness. Brightness is measured in cd/m². A highlight that's **rolled off** is eased down to the brightest level the picture can show, rather than cut off flat.
640	
641	| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
642	| --- | --- | --- |
643	| [Rec. 709 or untagged](#rec-709-and-untagged-sources) | Drawn as it is | Lifted to HDR reference white, so it looks the same |
644	| [HLG video](#hlg-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
645	| [PQ or HDR10 video](#pq-and-hdr10-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak | Real HDR, up to 1,000 cd/m² |
646	| [Wide-gamut SDR](#wide-gamut-sdr) | Converted to Rec. 709 | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
647	| [Camera log](#camera-log) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |
648	| [HLG or PQ still](#hdr-stills) | Converted as a video of the same kind is | Drawn in its own colour, as HDR |
649	| [Gain-map photo](#gain-map-photos) | Its ordinary picture | Its HDR highlights |
650	
651	## Rec. 709 and untagged sources
652	
653	Ordinary Rec. 709 video, video with no colour labels, recordings and stills are drawn as they are in an SDR project.
654	
655	In an HDR (HLG) project they're lifted to HDR reference white, the level ordinary white sits at: 203 cd/m², or 75 % of the HLG signal. They look the same as they do in SDR, and HDR highlights rise above them. Text, captions, shapes, graphics and the background colour are lifted the same way.
656	
657	## HLG video
658	
659	HLG video, such as iPhone HDR video, needs no setting. The file's own colour labels choose the conversion.
660	
661	- **In an SDR project** it's converted to Rec. 709 with its highlights rolled off smoothly. A colour Rec. 709 can't show is eased toward its own brightness instead of being clipped.
662	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it stays HLG, with its highlights above white intact. An HLG file over BT.2020 is used exactly as it is, and one over P3 or BT.709 primaries is converted into BT.2020.
663	
664	In an SDR project, HLG is converted whatever its primaries. A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020.
665	
666	## PQ and HDR10 video
667	
668	A PQ file, usually called HDR10, is always converted.
669	
670	- **In an SDR project** its highlights roll off to white at the peak read from the file. Colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness, as with HLG. You can override the peak in the Media tab's **HDR10** section. See [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/).
671	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it becomes real HDR, keeping its brightness up to 1,000 cd/m². If the file's peak is above that, its highlights are rolled off to fit. A peak of 1,000 cd/m² or less doesn't change the picture.
672	
673	A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020, as with HLG.
674	
675	## Wide-gamut SDR
676	
677	A source with BT.2020 or P3 D65 primaries and an SDR transfer curve, sRGB included, is converted to the project's colours rather than drawn with the wrong ones. This happens by itself, from the file's labels.
678	
679	- **In an SDR project** it's converted to Rec. 709. Colours Rec. 709 can't show are clipped.
680	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's converted into BT.2020 and lifted, so those colours survive.
681	
682	An SDR project always works in Rec. 709. To keep a wide-gamut source's colours, use an HDR (HLG) project.
683	
684	## sRGB-transfer files
685	
686	A source labelled with the sRGB transfer curve is read as sRGB rather than as Rec. 709. This is automatic too. Primaries that are absent or unrecognised read as BT.709.
687	
688	An sRGB file with BT.709 primaries never turns the conversion on by itself. It's read as sRGB when something else in the project needs converting, and it looks the same either way. With BT.2020 or P3 D65 primaries it counts as [wide-gamut SDR](#wide-gamut-sdr).
689	
690	## Full-range files
691	
692	A file stores its levels in video range, a narrower band of the available codes, or in full range, all of them. S-Log3 and V-Log files can be stored either way, and the two need reading differently. Frame Job takes the range from the file's full-range flag. If a VP9 video has no flag, it reads the range from the VP9 track's own settings. A file with neither is read as video range.
693	
694	Apple Log, Apple Log 2, C-Log2 and C-Log3 are read the same way whatever the flag says.
695	
696	:::caution
697	A non-ProRes Canon file flagged as video range that actually stores full-range codes looks too contrasty after C-Log2 or C-Log3 conversion.
698	:::
699	
700	## Camera log
701	
702	Log footage looks flat and grey until it's converted, and this is the one kind of source you may have to name. Frame Job recognises Apple Log and Apple Log 2 by themselves. For Sony, Panasonic and Canon footage, choose the curve in the Media tab's **Camera Log** section. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).
703	
704	- **In an SDR project** the footage becomes a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture.
705	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's converted to HLG instead of Rec. 709, with no highlight roll-off, so it's real HDR.
706	
707	## HDR stills
708	
709	A still labelled HLG or PQ is treated as HDR, the way a video of the same kind is, rather than being read as SDR. Bring it in with **File ▸ Add Media…** (<kbd>⇧⌘I</kbd>) as you would any picture. This works for PNG and HEIC, which keep their colour space and depth.
710	
711	- **In an SDR project** the still converts as an HLG or PQ video does.
712	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's drawn in its own colour, as HDR.
713	
714	Display P3, BT.709 and BT.2020 primaries are recognised, and any other reads as BT.2020.
715	
716	A PQ still has an [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/) like a PQ video. It takes a peak but no Camera Log.
717	
718	A still deeper than 8 bits per channel that isn't labelled HDR is an ordinary SDR picture, drawn at full depth. See [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).
719	
720	## Gain-map photos
721	
722	An iPhone HDR photo is a HEIC with a gain map: an ordinary picture plus the information to brighten its highlights. Frame Job reads ISO 21496-1 and Apple HDR gain maps.
723	
724	- **In an HDR (HLG) project** the photo shows its HDR highlights.
725	- **In an SDR project, and in every thumbnail,** it shows its ordinary picture.
726	
727	In the SDR version of an HDR project, the photo is its HDR rendition toned down, not the photo's own SDR image. That covers [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/), JPEG frames and SDR-version exports.
728	
729	A chroma key picked on a gain-map photo keys close to, but not exactly, what it keyed before a switch to HDR (HLG). Re-pick the key if an edge changes.
730	
731	## The same everywhere
732	
733	The conversion works the same way in the preview, in every export, and in rendered and saved frames.
734	
735	The timeline's filmstrip and the Media tab's thumbnails follow it too:
736	
737	- Filmstrips of log, PQ and HLG files show the converted picture, not the raw file. In an SDR project that's the picture in the preview. In an HDR (HLG) project they're drawn as an SDR project would draw them.
738	- An HLG or PQ still's thumbnail is drawn the same way. It appears a moment after import, once it's been converted.
739	- Changing a PQ file's peak redraws its strip, as changing a file's Camera Log does.
740	
741	**View ▸ Show Ungraded** (<kbd>⌃⌘U</kbd>) turns off the grades but leaves this conversion on, because the conversion is how the file is read, not part of the grade. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).
742	
743	## Good to know
744	
745	- Camera Log and the HDR10 peak belong to the file, not to a clip, so two clips of one file can't be read differently.
746	- SDR reference white in an HDR (HLG) project is fixed at 203 cd/m². There's no setting for it.
747	- A chroma key on HLG footage with P3 or BT.709 primaries, or on PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m², is close but not exact after a switch to HDR (HLG). [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/) has the detail.
748

756	=== log-luts.mdx
757	---
758	title: "Camera log from your own LUT"
759	description: "Convert a log file with a .cube LUT instead of a built-in curve, share that LUT between files, and remove it without surprises."
760	---
761	
762	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
763	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
764	
765	Log footage looks flat until it's converted. When [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) has no built-in curve for your footage, a `.cube` LUT, a file that maps one set of colours to another, can do the conversion instead. You pick the LUT once, and every clip of that file comes out as normal-looking video.
766	
767	<AtAGlance
768	  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ Use LUT…', 'Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ LUT: name']}
769	  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color', 'remove_media']}
770	/>
771	
772	## Use LUT…
773	
774	<Steps>
775	
776	1. Open the **Media** tab and click the video file in the list.
777	
778	2. In the **Camera Log** section, choose **Use LUT…** from the **Log** popup.
779	
780	3. Pick the `.cube` file. The panel asks you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709."
781	
782	</Steps>
783	
784	The LUT joins the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all as one undo step called **Camera Log**. The line under the popup and the section's header then read **LUT: name**.
785	
786	Frame Job takes the LUT's output as Rec. 709, so use a LUT made for that job. Like every Camera Log setting, it belongs to the file: every clip of the file follows it, reversed clips included, and it's applied before the chroma key and every grade.
787	
788	A file takes a curve or a LUT, not both, so choosing one replaces the other. A PQ file keeps its [peak override](/hdr/hdr10-peak/#undo-and-camera-log).
789	
790	If the file you pick is already in the Media list, Frame Job uses that entry and doesn't add a second one.
791	
792	The LUT has to be a 3D `.cube` of size 2 to 65 with the default 0 to 1 domain, and no larger than 32 MiB. Anything else shows an error naming the file and what's wrong with it, and nothing changes. For example: "“Film.cube” is not a LUT Frame Job reads: line 2: LUT_3D_SIZE 200 is outside 2–65." [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/) has the format in full.
793	
794	## A LUT already in the project
795	
796	Every `.cube` LUT in the project is listed in the **Log** popup as **LUT: name**, between the built-in curves and **Use LUT…**. The name is the file's name without `.cube`.
797	
798	To use the same LUT on another file, click that file in the list and choose its row. One LUT can convert any number of files.
799	
800	The popup and the [Look section](/color/looks/) read the same media list. A LUT you imported as a look is offered here, and a LUT you added with **Use LUT…** appears in the Look section's Imported group.
801	
802	To take a LUT off one file, choose **None** or a curve in the **Log** popup. The LUT stays in the Media list.
803	
804	## A LUT in use
805	
806	A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used, even when no clip has it as a look. **Unused only** hides it from the [Media list](/projects/media-tab/#unused-only), and **Remove** asks before it takes the LUT away.
807	
808	## Remove the LUT
809	
810	Right-click the LUT's row on the Media tab and choose **Remove**. The alert says what depends on it, for example:
811	
812	- "It is the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."
813	- "It is the look of 1 clip, which keeps its place and loses the look. …and the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."
814	
815	**Remove and Clear Looks** removes the LUT as one undo step, **Remove Media**. Those files go back to no conversion, so they show the log picture as recorded. Clips that had it as a look stay where they are and lose the look. A PQ file keeps its peak. **Cancel** changes nothing.
816	
817	The `.cube` file on your disk is never touched. See [Remove media](/projects/remove-media/).
818	
819	## Camera Log and looks
820	
821	Camera Log is applied before any look, so a look works on the picture the conversion made.
822	
823	If a clip's look is a `.cube` LUT and its file has a Camera Log, the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice."
824	
825	It's only a warning, and Frame Job changes nothing, because a creative LUT on top of a conversion is fine. If the look really is a camera LUT, keep it in one place: either in the **Log** popup or as the clip's look, not both.
826	
827	The eight built-in looks never show this warning. A `.cube` look on a PQ (HDR10) file does show it, even with **Log** set to **None**.
828	
829	## Good to know
830	
831	- In an HDR (HLG) project, a LUT's output is treated as SDR and [lifted to reference white](/hdr/dynamic-range/#sdr-material-in-an-hdr-project), so the file gains no HDR highlights. A built-in curve does become real HDR there.
832	- If the LUT can't be found or drawn, the footage shows unconverted, as flat log, until you [relink](/projects/relink-media/) the LUT. A LUT relinks like any other file in the Media list.
833	- Relinking the video file keeps its Camera Log.
834	- Camera Log is for video files. With an audio file, an image or a LUT selected, the popup is disabled and the line reads "Select a video in the list".
835	- **View ▸ Show Ungraded** turns looks and grades off and leaves the conversion on, because the conversion is how the file is read.
836	
837	## With an agent
838	
839	An agent takes two steps where a person takes one: `import_media` brings the `.cube` into the project, then `set_media_color` names it as the file's conversion, with `color` set to `{lut: <media id>}`. The call can't set a curve and a LUT together.
840	
841	`remove_media` won't take a LUT that's in use unless the call passes `with_clips: true`, which clears the conversions and looks that name it. See [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/).
842	
843	## Related
844	
845	- [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/)
846	- [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/)
847	- [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/)
848	- [Looks](/color/looks/)
849	- [The Media tab](/projects/media-tab/)
850	- [Remove media](/projects/remove-media/)
851	=== precision.mdx
852	---
853	title: "Precision and bit depth"
854	description: "How Frame Job keeps the depth of your footage through compositing and grading, which exports carry it, and what stays 8-bit."
855	---
856	
857	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
858	
859	Frame Job works in 16-bit float, so a gradient from a 10-bit camera file survives grading. There's nothing to turn on. This page says where that depth is kept and where it ends. "Deep" here means more than 8 bits per channel.
860	
861	<AtAGlance menu="File ▸ Export…" keys="⌘E" tools="export" />
862	
863	## 16-bit float compositing
864	
865	Every video source is decoded to 16-bit float, and every frame is composited at 16-bit float. Blends run there too, so a heavy grade keeps its precision. A 10-bit source keeps its detail all the way to a 10-bit or ProRes export.
866	
867	A 16-bit float frame takes twice the memory of an 8-bit one, so an export needs about twice the memory for its frames.
868	
869	## 10-bit exports
870	
871	The format you choose on the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/) decides how much of that depth reaches the file.
872	
873	| Format | Depth in the file |
874	| --- | --- |
875	| **HEVC 10-bit (MP4)** | 10-bit (Main 10) |
876	| **AV1 (MP4)**, **AV1 (WebM)** | Always 10-bit |
877	| **ProRes 422 (MOV)**, **ProRes 4444 (MOV)** | Deep: they take the composited frames as they are, at 10 bits in ProRes 422 and 12 in ProRes 4444. See [ProRes](/export/prores/). |
878	| **VP9 (WebM)** | 8-bit for an SDR picture, 10-bit for HLG and HDR10 |
879	| **H.264 (MP4)**, **HEVC (MP4)**, **HEVC with Alpha (MOV)**, **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** | 8-bit |
880	| **Animated GIF**, **Animated PNG** | 8-bit |
881	
882	The sheet's **Bit depth:** row is about sound, not the picture. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/).
883	
884	## Deep stills
885	
886	A still deeper than 8 bits per channel, such as a 16-bit PNG or TIFF or a 10-bit HEIC, is drawn at 16-bit float. An 8-bit still is drawn at 8 bits. It's automatic and there's no setting: add the file with **File ▸ Add Media…** (<kbd>⇧⌘I</kbd>) as usual.
887	
888	## Saved frames
889	
890	**File ▸ Save Frame…** (<kbd>⌥⌘E</kbd>) writes a 16-bit PNG or a 10-bit HEIC when the frame shows a deep still or a 10-bit VP9 clip, and always in an HDR (HLG) project. A 10-bit HEVC or ProRes clip gets the same, when every video track in the timeline is that deep. A JPEG is always 8-bit. See [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).
891	
892	## Reversed clips
893	
894	A reversed clip plays from a backwards copy rendered at 10 bits, at the source's exact size and with the source's own colour labels, so an HDR or log clip still reads correctly. See [Reverse a clip](/speed/reverse/).
895	
896	## What stays 8-bit
897	
898	Text, shapes, captions, graphics and screen recordings are 8-bit, and so are thumbnails. In an HDR (HLG) project those layers are still [lifted to HDR reference white](/hdr/dynamic-range/), so they sit with the rest of the picture.
899	
900	## Related

909	---
910	title: "Show SDR Version"
911	description: "Preview an HDR project as its SDR version, the picture 8-bit formats, JPEG frames and the SDR export get, without changing anything."
912	---
913	
914	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
915	
916	An HDR project also has an SDR version: the picture it writes to formats that can't carry HDR. Show SDR Version puts that picture in the preview, so you can check it before you export.
917	
918	<AtAGlance
919	  menu="View ▸ Show SDR Version"
920	  where="The SDR Version tag at the preview's top left"
921	  tools="render_frame"
922	/>
923	
924	## Show the SDR version
925	
926	Choose **View ▸ Show SDR Version**. A checkmark shows it's on, and choosing it again turns it off. It has no keyboard shortcut, and it's always available.
927	
928	The preview then shows the picture these outputs get:
929	
930	- The 8-bit formats: H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, VP9 with Alpha (WebM), Animated GIF and Animated PNG.
931	- JPEG frames from [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).
932	- The **SDR version** choice on the [10-bit export formats](/hdr/export-hdr/).
933	
934	While it's on, the [scopes](/hdr/hdr-scopes/) read the SDR version too.
935	
936	In an SDR project the picture already is the SDR version, so no pixel changes.
937	
938	## The tag
939	
940	A tag reading "SDR Version" sits in the preview's top-left corner while the view is on. It comes after the **Ungraded** and **Selection** tags when those are on. It shows in an SDR project too.
941	
942	You can still click and drag on the canvas through the tag.
943	
944	## It belongs to the window
945	
946	Show SDR Version is a way of looking, not an edit. It reaches the [preview](/timeline/preview/) and the [Preview Window](/timeline/preview-window/) (**View ▸ Preview Window**, <kbd>⇧⌘P</kbd>), and never an export or a saved frame.
947	
948	It isn't remembered either, so a new window starts with it off.
949	
950	## What the SDR version is
951	
952	The SDR version brings the HLG master back to Rec. 709.
953	
954	- The picture comes back as it was, up to a little below HDR reference white, the level ordinary white sits at.
955	- A soft roll-off starts there, so a white title stays white, at about 248 of 255.
956	- Highlights above reference white are rolled off, and reach full white at 1,000 cd/m².
957	
958	A [gain-map photo](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/#gain-map-photos) comes from its HDR picture toned down here, not from the ordinary picture stored in it.
959	
960	## With an agent
961	
962	`render_frame` draws any frame as the SDR version when the call passes `sdr_version: true`. The default is `false`. The menu item itself never reaches the tool, so it makes no difference whether it's on. An SDR project's frame comes out identical either way, because it's already its own SDR version. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/#sdr_version).
963	
964	## Related
965

967	- [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/)
968	- [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/)
969	- [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/)

1	---
2	title: "Tools: picture and grade (set_video)"
3	description: Change a clip's position, crop, effects, cut-out, cursor, motion and grade from an agent with one patch tool, set_video.
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	`set_video` is the one tool behind everything a clip's picture does: where it sits, how it's cropped, its effects, its motion and its grade. It takes a list of clips and a patch, an object holding only the properties you want to change. This page lists every key a patch can hold.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  tools="set_video"
12	  where={['Clip tab ▸ Picture sub-tab', 'Clip tab ▸ Color sub-tab', 'Dragging on the canvas']}
13	/>
14	
15	## `set_video`
16	
17	Merges a patch into each clip's own video properties, as one undo step however many clips it names. It mirrors the Clip tab's [Picture sub-tab](/canvas/picture-tab/) and [Color sub-tab](/color/color-tab/).
18	
19	| Argument | Type | Required | What it does |
20	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
21	| `clips` | array of integers | Yes | The clips to change, at least one. `get_project` lists their ids. |
22	| `patch` | object | Yes | The properties to change. The rest of this page lists its keys. |
23	| `scope` | integer | No | A nest id, to edit inside that nest. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/). |
24	| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on, as `get_project` reports it. Leave it out for the frontmost one. |
25	
26	```json
27	{ "clips": [12, 14], "patch": { "opacity": 0.8, "shadow": { "blur": 20 } } }
28	```
29	
30	**How a patch merges.** A key you leave out keeps its value, inside a nested object too, so `{shadow: {blur: 20}}` keeps the shadow's colour, angle and distance. On a clip that has no shadow yet, the keys you left out take the defaults listed below. `shadow`, `chroma`, `reflection`, `spotlight`, `motion`, `look`, `cursor`, `cutout` and `hide_silent` set to `null` clear that property. `filters` and `obscure` are lists, so each replaces whole: send the full list, or `[]` to clear it. See [Patches](/mcp/patches/).
31	
32	**Colours.** A colour is four numbers, `[r, g, b, a]`, each 0 to 1. Three numbers are refused, and so is a value outside the range. Two keys differ: the chroma key's colour is three numbers with no alpha, and the cursor's `click_color` is a CSS colour.
33	
34	**What it answers.** `ok` and the `project` summary. If the patch changes nothing, the call says so and leaves no undo step. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
35	
36	**When it refuses.**
37	
38	- A key or value the patch doesn't know is an error naming its dotted path, array indices included, and the value you sent, such as `filters[1].kind`. Nothing is dropped, corrected or clamped.
39	- A number outside its range is an error naming the key, the range and the number.
40	- A clip with no video properties is an error: "clip 7 has no video properties".
41	- The sections below list what a particular kind of clip can't take.
42	
43	### Which key does what
44	
45	| Keys | Section |
46	| --- | --- |
47	| `x`, `y`, `scale`, `rotation`, `opacity`, `blend` | [Transform](#transform-position-scale-rotation-opacity-and-blend) |
48	| `crop`, `corner_radius` | [Crop and corners](#crop-and-corners) |
49	| `shadow`, `chroma`, `filters`, `reflection`, `spotlight`, `obscure` | [Effects](#effects-shadow-chroma-key-filters-reflection-spotlight-and-obscure) |
50	| `cutout` | [Remove Background](#cutout) |
51	| `behind_subject` | [Text Behind Subject](#behind_subject) |
52	| `cursor` | [The recorded cursor](#cursor) |
53	| `motion` | [Motion presets](#motion) |
54	| `motion_blur` | [Motion blur](#motion_blur) |
55	| `hide_silent` | [Hide While Silent](#hide_silent) |
56	| `color`, `wheels`, `curves`, `look`, `qualifier` | [Light and colour](#color), [wheels](#wheels), [curves](#curves), [looks and LUTs](#look), [the qualifier](#qualifier) |
57	
58	### On an adjustment clip
59	
60	An [adjustment clip](/color/adjustment-clips/) has no picture of its own. Only `color`, `wheels`, `curves`, `look`, the sepia, noir, vignette and invert filters, and `opacity` (the grade's strength) do anything there, and `qualifier` narrows which pixels they reach. The blur, sharpen and pixelate filters and any blend mode are errors, such as "clip 7 is an adjustment clip and cannot take the blur filter".
61	
62	### Animate a property
63	
64	`set_video` changes the clip's base value, which holds for the clip's whole length. To change a value over time, use `add_action` then `set_action_end`. See [Tools: animation](/mcp/tools-animation/). `motion` and `hide_silent` can't be animated.
65	
66	## Transform: position, scale, rotation, opacity and blend
67	
68	The clip's picture is centred on the canvas centre plus `x` and `y`, scaled, then rotated about that same centre. The [Transform section](/canvas/transform/) and dragging on the canvas change the same values.
69	
70	| Key | What it does | Range |
71	| --- | --- | --- |
72	| `x`, `y` | The clip's centre, in canvas pixels from the canvas centre. `y` runs down. | Any number |
73	| `scale` | The size. 1 is native pixels. | 0.01 to 10 |
74	| `rotation` | Degrees about the clip's centre. Positive turns clockwise on screen. | Any number |
75	| `opacity` | How solid the clip is. | 0 to 1 |
76	| `blend` | How the clip combines with what's already on the canvas. | `normal`, `multiply`, `screen`, `add`, `overlay`, `darken`, `lighten`, `difference` |
77	
78	`normal` is the default. A blend mode needs something under it. Over an empty black canvas, `multiply`, `darken` and `overlay` read black, while `screen`, `add`, `lighten` and `difference` change nothing, so `add_background` is usually the call to make first.
79	
80	A blend is forced to `normal` for the length of any transition, and on a clip on a matte track, so the frame there can differ from the value `get_project` reports. A nest clip can't take a blend mode other than `normal`. See [Blend modes](/canvas/blend-modes/).
81	
82	## Crop and corners
83	
84	| Key | What it does | Range |
85	| --- | --- | --- |
86	| `crop` | `{l, t, r, b}`, the pixels to remove from each edge of the source. Cropping never shifts what's left. | Each 0 or more |
87	| `corner_radius` | Rounds the corners of the cropped picture, in source pixels, before it's rotated. | 0 or more |
88	
89	The opposite edges have to leave something behind: `l` plus `r` must be less than the source's width, and `t` plus `b` less than its height. See [Crop](/canvas/crop/) and [Corner radius](/canvas/corner-radius/).
90	
91	## Effects: shadow, chroma key, filters, reflection, spotlight and obscure
92	
93	Each of these is off until you set it. `shadow`, `chroma`, `reflection` and `spotlight` are objects that merge, and `null` clears one. `filters` and `obscure` are lists that replace whole.
94	
95	### Shadow
96	
97	`shadow` is `null` or an object. See [Shadow](/effects/shadow/).
98	
99	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
100	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
101	| `color` | The shadow's colour. | Four numbers | Black |
102	| `opacity` | How strong it is. | 0 to 1 | 0.5 |
103	| `blur` | How soft it is, in source pixels. | 0 or more | 12 |
104	| `angle` | The direction, in degrees. 0 is to the right, turning anticlockwise. | Any number | 315 |
105	| `distance` | How far it falls, in source pixels. | 0 or more | 8 |
106	
107	### Chroma key
108	
109	`chroma` is `null` or an object. See [Chroma Key](/effects/chroma-key/).
110	
111	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
112	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
113	| `key` | The colour to remove, as three numbers with no alpha. | Each 0 to 1 | Green, `[0, 1, 0]` |
114	| `tolerance` | How far from the key a colour can be and still go. | 0 to 1 | 0.2 |
115	| `softness` | How gradually the edge falls off. | 0 to 1 | 0.1 |
116	| `spill` | How much of the key's colour to take off what's left. | 0 to 1 | 0.5 |
117	
118	### Filters
119	
120	`filters` is a list of up to four `{kind, amount}` objects. `kind` is `blur`, `sharpen`, `pixelate`, `sepia`, `noir`, `vignette` or `invert`. `amount` is 0 to 1, where 0 does nothing. Each entry must name both keys: leaving one out is an error. A fifth filter is an error, never dropped. Sepia, noir, vignette and invert run in list order. Blur, sharpen and pixelate always run before them, wherever they sit in the list. See [Filters](/effects/filters/).
121	
122	```json
123	{ "filters": [{ "kind": "noir", "amount": 1 }, { "kind": "vignette", "amount": 0.4 }] }
124	```
125	
126	### Reflection
127	
128	`reflection` is `null` or an object. See [Reflection](/effects/reflection/).
129	
130	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
131	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
132	| `opacity` | How strong the reflection is where it touches the clip. | 0 to 1 | 0.35 |
133	| `height` | How much of the clip is mirrored, as a fraction of its cropped height. | 0 to 1 | 0.5 |
134	| `gap` | The space between the clip and the reflection, in source pixels. | 0 or more | 0 |
135	| `falloff` | How fast it fades, as a fraction of the cropped height. 0 doesn't fade, and 1 reaches transparent exactly at `height`. | 0 to 1 | 1 |
136	
137	### Spotlight
138	
139	`spotlight` is `null` or an object. It dims everything outside a shape and can magnify what's inside it. See [Spotlight](/effects/spotlight/).
140	
141	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
142	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
143	| `shape` | The shape. | `rect`, `ellipse` | `rect` |
144	| `x`, `y` | The shape's centre, in source pixels from the centre of the cropped picture, `y` down. It can sit outside the picture. | Any number | 0 |
145	| `width`, `height` | The shape's size, in source pixels. | Above 0 | 480, 270 |
146	| `feather` | How many source pixels the edge blurs over. | 0 or more | 40 |
147	| `dim` | How much darker it is outside. 0 changes nothing, and 1 is black. | 0 to 1 | 0.6 |
148	| `zoom` | How much to magnify what's inside. 1 is no zoom. | 1 to 2 | 1 |
149	
150	Because the box is in source pixels, it stays on the picture when the clip is moved, scaled or rotated.
151	
152	### Obscure
153	
154	`obscure` is a list of up to four regions, each hiding what's under it. It uses the spotlight's frame for its centre and box. See [Obscure](/effects/obscure/).
155	
156	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
157	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
158	| `shape` | The shape. | `rect`, `ellipse` | `rect` |
159	| `x`, `y` | The region's centre, in source pixels from the centre of the cropped picture. | Any number | 0 |
160	| `width`, `height` | The region's size, in source pixels. | Above 0 | 480, 270 |
161	| `feather` | How many source pixels the effect ramps in over. | 0 or more | 20 |
162	| `kind` | How it hides. | `blur`, `pixelate` | `pixelate` |
163	| `amount` | How strongly it hides. | 0 to 1 | 1 |
164	
165	## `cutout`
166	
167	Remove Background: draws the clip as its subject alone, from masks made on your Mac. It mirrors **Clip ▸ Remove Background** and the Picture sub-tab's **Background** section. See [Remove Background](/effects/remove-background/).
168	
169	`cutout` is `null` or an object. `{cutout: {}}` turns it on with all five defaults, an object merges, and `null` removes it.
170	
171	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
172	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
173	| `subject` | What to keep. `foreground` is the picture's foreground object, and only an image clip can take it. | `person`, `foreground` | `person` |
174	| `quality` | The mask quality. Only `standard` works, and `best` is refused. | `standard` | `standard` |
175	| `background` | `remove` draws only the subject. `keep` draws the clip whole, which [Text Behind Subject](#behind_subject) uses. | `remove`, `keep` | `remove` |
176	| `edge` | Shrinks or grows the outline. | −1 to 1 | 0 |
177	| `feather` | Softens the outline. | 0 to 1 | 0 |
178	
179	A media, still or image clip can take a cutout. A text, shape, graphic, adjustment or nest clip is refused, and so is `foreground` on a media or still clip.
180	
181	**When the masks are made.** They're made as soon as the cutout is set, and `analyze_cutout` says where they stand. See [Tools: reading analysis](/mcp/tools-analysis/). The cut-out draws in the preview, `render_frame` and every export:
182	
183	- The preview draws a frame whole while its mask isn't made yet.
184	- `render_frame` waits up to 30 s for its masks, then draws the clip uncut and says so.
185	- An export waits for every mask it draws.
186	- A stretch of the clip where no person was found draws uncut.
187	
188	**In an action.** `edge` and `feather` animate, and `background` switches when the action ends. `subject` and `quality` are refused there, and an action can't switch the cutout off. On a clip with no cutout, an action's cutout keys do nothing.
189	
190	## `behind_subject`
191	
192	Text Behind Subject: `true` makes the person in a cut-out clip stand in front of this clip, by cutting this clip away wherever that person is at each moment. It looks at every cut-out clip on a track behind it, on the same timeline or in the same nest, and inside any nest on such a track. A cut-out clip in front of it doesn't cut it. Any clip with a `cutout` counts, with `background` set to `remove` or `keep`. The default is `false`. It mirrors the Picture sub-tab's **Behind Subject** section. See [Text Behind Subject](/effects/text-behind-subject/).
193	
194	Any clip that draws a picture can take it, except an adjustment clip or a nest clip, which are refused. In an action it switches when the action ends. [`text_behind_subject`](/mcp/tools-clip-properties/) places a title this way in one step.
195	
196	## `cursor`
197	
198	Styles the pointer Frame Job recorded beside a screen recording, in the movie's [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/), as it's drawn on this clip. It mirrors the Picture sub-tab's **Cursor** section. See [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/).
199	
200	`cursor` is `null` or an object. `{cursor: {}}` stores all eight defaults, and an object merges. A value out of range is refused, never clamped.
201	
202	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
203	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
204	| `show` | Whether the cursor is drawn. | `true`, `false` | `true` |
205	| `scale` | Its size. | 0.25 to 8 | 1 |
206	| `style` | `recorded` draws the recorded image, and `arrow` draws Frame Job's own arrow. `recorded` also draws the arrow at a moment the file holds no cursor image. | `recorded`, `arrow` | `recorded` |
207	| `smoothing` | How much the path is smoothed. | 0 to 1 | 0 |
208	| `hide_idle` | Seconds of no activity before it hides. `null` never hides it. | `null`, 0.5 to 30 | `null` |
209	| `clicks` | What a click draws. | `none`, `ripple` | `none` |
210	| `click_color` | The ripple's colour, as a CSS colour. | Any CSS colour | `#ffffffcc` |
211	| `click_size` | The ripple's size. | 0.25 to 4 | 1 |
212	
213	**In an action.** `scale` and `click_size` animate. `show`, `style`, `clicks` and `click_color` switch when the action ends. `smoothing` and `hide_idle` have no effect in an action, so write them here. On a clip with no cursor, every cursor key in an action switches at the end, so give the clip one first with `{cursor: {}}` if you want them to animate.
214	
215	## `motion`
216	
217	What the clip does on its way in, on its way out and all the way through. It mirrors **Clip ▸ Motion ▸**. See [Motion presets](/motion/motion-presets/).
218	
219	`motion` is `null` or `{in, out, during}`. The three slots merge: a slot you leave out keeps what's stored, a slot set to `null` clears that slot, and `{motion: null}` clears all three.
220	
221	| Slot | Keys | Values |
222	| --- | --- | --- |
223	| `in`, `out` | `kind`, `duration` | `kind` is `fade`, `zoom_in`, `zoom_out`, `slide_left`, `slide_right`, `slide_up`, `slide_down`, `spin` or `pop`. `duration` is in ticks, measured from the clip's first or last frame. |
224	| `during` | `kind`, `amount`, `period` | `kind` is `pulse`, `shake`, `spin`, `bounce` or `drift`. `amount` is 0 to 1. `period` is in ticks, and `drift` ignores it. |
225	
226	```json
227	{ "motion": { "in": { "kind": "fade", "duration": 300000 }, "during": null } }
228	```
229	
230	A slot you name without its keys starts from a half-second `fade`, or for `during` a `pulse` of amount 0.5 and period 1 s.
231	
232	The durations snap to the frame grid, and the period snaps with a floor of one frame, so `get_project` can answer with a number near the one you sent. `in` plus `out` longer than the clip scales both down to meet, rather than being refused. A negative duration, or a period under one tick, is an error.
233	
234	`motion` can't be animated: `set_action_end` refuses it. `get_project` reports the clip as if it weren't moving, because the preset only becomes placement when a frame is drawn.
235	
236	## `motion_blur`
237	
238	Blurs the clip, and its moving cursor, along their motion. It mirrors the **Motion Blur** row in the Picture sub-tab's **Transform** section. See [Motion blur](/motion/motion-blur/).
239	
240	`motion_blur` is 0 to 1, the shutter as a fraction of one canvas frame. 0 is off and the default, and 0.5 is a 180° shutter. It animates in an action, and draws in the preview, `render_frame` and every export.
241	
242	Anything above 0 is refused on a nest clip, so set it on the clips inside, and on an adjustment clip. The clip draws sharp during a transition, including inside a nest clip that's in one, on a matte track or cut by a matte, when Behind Subject cuts it, and with a drop shadow. The value stays stored. See [Where it stays sharp](/motion/motion-blur/#where-it-stays-sharp).
243	
244	## `hide_silent`
245	
246	Fades a clip, usually a camera, out while a media's speech is silent, and back in ahead of the next words. It mirrors the Picture sub-tab's **Hide While Silent** section. See [Hide While Silent](/effects/hide-while-silent/).
247	
248	`hide_silent` is `null` or an object.
249	
250	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
251	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
252	| `media` | Required. The id of the media, with sound, whose speech the clip follows. | A media id | |
253	| `pre_roll` | How long before speech the clip is fully in, in ticks. | 0 to 3,000,000 (5 s) | 120,000 (0.2 s) |
254	| `hold` | How long after speech it stays, in ticks. | 0 to 3,000,000 (5 s) | 900,000 (1.5 s) |
255	| `fade` | How long the fade takes, in ticks. | 0 to 3,000,000 (5 s) | 180,000 (0.3 s) |
256	
257	```json
258	{ "hide_silent": { "media": 3, "hold": 600000 } }
259	```
260	
261	The fade follows the clips of that media on the clip's own timeline or nest, then in each nest around it, working outwards until it finds one playing. Where none plays, the clip stays visible. These three times don't snap to the frame grid.
262	
263	If the media has no saved speech, this call saves it from the on-device voice detection first, in the same undo step. It's refused when the media has no sound, when its speech hasn't been detected yet ("Try again in a moment."), and on a nest clip, so set it on the clips inside.
264	
265	Only the drawn frame sees the fade: `get_project` reads the clip's opacity without it. `hide_silent` can't be animated.
266	
267	## `color`
268	
269	The thirteen values of the Color sub-tab's **Light** and **Color** sections, in one object. Each is 0 for unchanged, and any subset merges. See [Light](/color/light/) and [Brightness, contrast, saturation and hue](/color/color-section/).
270	
271	| Key | What it does | Range |
272	| --- | --- | --- |
273	| `exposure` | Exposure, in stops. | −3 to 3 |
274	| `temperature` | Positive is warmer. | −1 to 1 |
275	| `tint` | Positive is more magenta. | −1 to 1 |
276	| `highlights` | The upper half of the brightness range. | −1 to 1 |
277	| `shadows` | The lower half of the brightness range. | −1 to 1 |
278	| `whites` | Stretches the picture, held at black. | −1 to 1 |
279	| `blacks` | Stretches the picture, held at white. | −1 to 1 |
280	| `vibrance` | Saturation on the colours that have little. | −1 to 1 |
281	| `fade` | Lifts black towards 10 % and lowers white towards 95 %. | 0 to 1 |
282	| `brightness` | Brightness. | Any number. The inspector's row runs −1 to 1. |
283	| `contrast` | Contrast. | Any number. The inspector's row runs −1 to 1. |
284	| `saturation` | Saturation. | Any number. The inspector's row runs −1 to 1. |
285	| `hue` | Turns every colour's hue this many degrees, red towards yellow towards green, keeping its brightness. | Any number. The inspector's row runs −180 to 180. |
286	
287	A value outside a stated range is refused.
288	
289	The grade runs in this order: `color`, `wheels`, `curves`, `look`, then the sepia, noir, vignette and invert filters.
290	
291	## `wheels`
292	
293	Lift, gamma and gain: three colour pushes, each with its own brightness. An agent can set a push as exact numbers, which the [Wheels section](/color/wheels/) has no field for.
294	
295	`wheels` is `{lift, gamma, gain}`, each `{x, y, master}`, each −1 to 1, with 0 unchanged. Any subset merges, so `{wheels: {lift: {x: 0.2, y: -0.1}}}` keeps lift's `master` and the other two wheels.
296	
297	| Key | What it does |
298	| --- | --- |
299	| `x`, `y` | The colour push. Its angle is the hue (0° red, 120° green, 240° blue), and its length is the strength. It must lie inside the unit circle, so `x²` plus `y²` is at most 1. |
300	| `master` | The brightness. |
301	
302	`lift` moves black and holds white, `gain` moves white and holds black, and `gamma` moves the middle and holds both ends. A value outside these limits is refused, never clamped.
303	
304	## `curves`
305	
306	Writes the curves of the Color sub-tab's **Curves** section, one list of points per channel. See [Master and RGB curves](/color/curves/) and [Hue vs Hue and Hue vs Sat curves](/color/hue-curves/).
307	
308	`curves` is an object with up to six channels. A list replaces that channel whole, and `null` removes it. Each list is 2 to 16 `[x, y]` points with `x` strictly rising.
309	
310	| Channel | `x` | `y` | No change |
311	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
312	| `master`, `red`, `green`, `blue` | 0 to 1 | 0 to 1 | `y` equals `x` from 0 to 1 |
313	| `hue_hue` | Hue in degrees, 0 up to but not including 360 | A shift in degrees, −180 to 180 | Every `y` is 0 |
314	| `hue_sat` | Hue in degrees, 0 up to but not including 360 | A saturation gain, 0 to 2 | Every `y` is 1 |
315	
316	```json
317	{ "curves": { "master": [[0, 0.05], [0.5, 0.55], [1, 1]], "hue_sat": null } }
318	```
319	
320	A curve that changes nothing is stored as no curve. A point outside these limits is refused, never clamped.
321	
322	The tone channels are smooth monotone curves through their points, flat outside the first and last `x`, and a colour goes through `master` first, then its own channel. The two hue curves are smooth curves that wrap at 0 and 360. They run after the tone channels, and both look up the colour's original hue, so `hue_sat` doesn't see the shift `hue_hue` made. A positive shift turns red towards yellow towards green, keeping brightness, and the gain scales saturation. Greys are left alone: a colour whose strongest and weakest channels are within 0.02 of each other doesn't change, and the effect reaches full strength at 0.06.
323	
324	In an action, a curve that changes nothing animates to neutral, and two curves with different point counts blend their values across the action.
325	
326	## `look`
327	
328	Applies one of the eight built-in looks, or an imported `.cube` LUT, at an amount. It mirrors the Color sub-tab's **Look** section and **Clip ▸ Look ▸**. See [Looks](/color/looks/) and [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/).
329	
330	`look` is `null` or an object. `{look: null}` removes it.
331	
332	| Key | What it does | Range | Default |
333	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
334	| `kind` | Which look. | `warm`, `cool`, `teal_orange`, `vivid`, `faded`, `vintage`, `dramatic`, `black_white`, `lut` | |
335	| `media` | The media id of the `.cube` file. Required with `lut`, and refused with any other kind. | A LUT's media id | |
336	| `amount` | How much of it. | 0 to 1 | 1 |
337	
338	```json
339	{ "look": { "kind": "teal_orange", "amount": 0.6 } }
340	```
341	
342	For a LUT, bring the file in with `import_media`, then send `{look: {kind: "lut", media: 9}}` with the id it answers.
343	
344	A new kind keeps the clip's amount, and a built-in kind replaces a LUT. An amount alone needs a clip that already has a look. In an action the amount animates, and a change of kind or of LUT switches when the action ends.
345	
346	## `qualifier`
347	
348	Narrows which pixels an adjustment clip's grade reaches, by hue, saturation and luma. It mirrors the Color sub-tab's **Qualifier** section. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).
349	
350	The qualifier is for adjustment clips only. On any other clip it's an error naming the clip. It reads the picture behind the clip, before the grade.
351	
352	`qualifier` is `{hue, saturation, luma, invert, blur}`.
353	
354	| Key | Keys inside it | What it does |
355	| --- | --- | --- |
356	| `hue` | `center`, `width`, `softness` | In degrees. `center` is 0 to 360 and wraps. `width` is 0 to 360, fully selected about the centre. `softness` is 0 to 180, the fall-off outside each edge. A colour's selection fades out as its chroma falls from 0.06 to 0.02, and at 0.02 or under it's never selected. |
357	| `saturation` | `low`, `high`, `softness` | Each 0 to 1, with `low` no more than `high`. Near-black reads as 0. |
358	| `luma` | `low`, `high`, `softness` | Each 0 to 1, with `low` no more than `high`. Rec. 709 luma, or BT.2020 luma in an HLG project. |
359	| `invert` | | `true` selects everything else. |
360	| `blur` | | 0 to 1, 0 being off. Softens the selection by a Gaussian of 24 × `blur` canvas pixels. It never softens a matte cutting the clip, and does nothing while no range is on. |
361	
362	A range merges: `{hue: {}}` turns hue on at centre 30, width 50, softness 25, and saturation and luma turn on at low 0, high 1, softness 0.1. A partial range keeps the rest, and `null` turns a range off. The selection is the product of the ranges that are on. A value outside its bounds is refused, never clamped.
363	
364	In an action the numbers animate, the hue centre taking the short way round, so 350 to 10 passes 0. A range turned on or off, and `invert`, switch when the action ends.
365	
366	`render_frame` with `selection` set to the adjustment clip's id draws what the qualifier selects, as [Show Selection](/color/show-selection/) does. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).

2	title: "Histogram"
3	description: "See how a frame's tones are spread from black to white, and read how much of the picture is clipped at each end."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	The histogram shows how a frame's tones are spread: how much of the picture is dark, how much is bright, and whether either end has run out of room. Use it to judge exposure and contrast, and to catch clipping while you grade.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  menu="View ▸ Scopes"
12	  keys="⌃⌘W"
13	  where="The Scopes panel ▸ a slot's pop-up ▸ Histogram"
14	  tools="render_frame"
15	/>
16	
17	## Open the histogram
18	
19	Choose **View ▸ Scopes**, then pick **Histogram** from a slot's pop-up. Neither slot opens on it, because a new window starts with **Waveform** over **Vectorscope**. The choice lasts while the window is open. See [Scopes](/color/scopes/) for the panel itself.
20	
21	## Read the histogram
22	
23	Levels run from 0 on the left to 255 on the right, so black is at the left edge and white is at the right. The height at each level is how many pixels sit there.
24	
25	Red, green and blue are drawn as translucent tinted fills, and luma, the picture's brightness, is a white line on top.
26	
27	| What you see | What it tells you |
28	| --- | --- |
29	| A pile against the left edge | Shadows are crushed to black |
30	| A pile against the right edge | Highlights are clipped to white |
31	| Empty space at both ends | A flat picture, with room to add contrast in [Light](/color/light/) or [Curves](/color/curves/) |
32	| One colour's fill sitting to the side of the others | That channel is brighter or darker overall, which often means a colour cast |
33	
34	Heights are on a logarithmic scale, so a small count still shows up beside a big one, and a peak twice as tall holds far more than twice the pixels. All four share one scale, set by the tallest count in any of them, so you can compare them directly.
35	
36	## Clipping readouts
37	
38	Two readouts sit below the histogram:
39	
40	- **Highlights clipped** is the share of the frame at the very top level, 255.
41	- **Shadows clipped** is the share at the very bottom level, 0.
42	
43	They read like "Highlights clipped 1.9 %", to one decimal place, and show "—" until a frame has been measured. The [Waveform](/color/waveform-and-parade/) shows the same two figures.
44	
45	Both are measured on luma, so read them with these in mind:
46	
47	- A single colour channel can clip while luma doesn't. Watch the fills at the right edge, or use the [Parade](/color/waveform-and-parade/), to catch that.
48	- They count the whole frame. Black canvas around a smaller picture, or letterbox bars, counts towards **Shadows clipped**.
49	
50	## Good to know
51	
52	- The histogram measures the frame the preview composes, so it follows playback, your edits and [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/). It changes nothing in the project or in an export.
53	- The slot's caption says what the scope reads: "Rec. 709 · encoded", the picture's own encoded values. In an HDR (HLG) project it reads "Rec. 2100 HLG", and luma is worked out for that colour space. With **Show SDR Version** on, the scope reads that SDR picture as it would in an SDR project. See [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/).
54	- The histogram is 140 pt tall. If the preview area is too short for both slots, it shrinks with them. Under 360 pt tall, only the top slot shows.
55	
56	## With an agent
57	
58	`render_frame` measures a frame's histogram as numbers when an agent passes `histogram: true`, which is off by default. The reply says what share of the frame clips high and low by luma. The counts for red, green, blue and luma at each of the 256 levels, and both percentages, go to a `.histogram.json` file beside the image. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).
59

7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
9	
10	The vectorscope shows a frame's colour with its brightness taken away: which hues are in the picture and how strong they are. Use it to spot a colour cast, to check skin tones, and to see how far a grade has pushed saturation.
11	
12	<AtAGlance
13	  menu="View ▸ Scopes"
14	  keys="⌃⌘W"
15	  where="The Scopes panel ▸ a slot's pop-up ▸ Vectorscope"
16	  tools="render_frame"
17	/>
18	
19	<Shot
20	  name="04b-preview-scopes.preview"
21	  alt="The preview with the Scopes panel beside it. The bottom slot shows the Vectorscope, a near-black square with six labelled target boxes around it, R at the top, Mg top right, B right, Cy at the bottom, G bottom left and Yl left. A line runs from the centre cross up and to the left, and a thin white trace runs from the centre towards the B box, for the blue card in the picture. The 1×, 2× and 4× cells sit in the bottom-right corner, with 1× filled."
22	/>
23	
24	## Open the vectorscope
25	
26	Choose **View ▸ Scopes**. In a new window the panel starts with **Waveform** on top and **Vectorscope** below. If a slot shows something else, pick **Vectorscope** from its pop-up. Both slots can show it, each at its own zoom. See [Scopes](/color/scopes/) for the panel itself.
27	
28	## Read the trace
29	
30	Every pixel in the frame lands somewhere on the near-black square, and the white trace is all of them together.
31	
32	- **The centre is no colour.** Greys, black and white all sit on the faint cross.
33	- **Distance from the centre is strength.** A pale colour stays close in, and a saturated one reaches out towards the edge.
34	- **Direction is hue.** The [targets](#the-targets) show which way each colour lies.
35	- **Brightness is how many pixels are there.** The scale is logarithmic, so a small patch of colour still shows up beside a large one.
36	
37	The two axes are the colour-difference signals: Cb runs across and Cr runs up. The scope draws no circles and has no readouts, so the targets and the skin line are your only references.
38	
39	A picture with no colour cast keeps its neutral areas on the cross. If something that should be grey sits to one side of it, the picture leans the way the trace leans. [Zoom in](#zoom-in-on-a-low-saturation-picture) to see a small cast.
40	
41	## The targets
42	
43	Six boxes mark where 75 % colour bars land, so you can tell which way a colour lies and how strong it is. Each label sits outside its box, away from the centre.
44	
45	| Label | Colour | Where it sits |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| R | Red | Up, a little left |
48	| Mg | Magenta | Up and right |
49	| B | Blue | Right, a little down |
50	| Cy | Cyan | Down, a little right |
51	| G | Green | Down and left |
52	| Yl | Yellow | Left, a little up |
53	
54	## The skin line
55	
56	The line running out from the centre, up and to the left, marks where skin tones fall. It's drawn at the hue of a standard light-skin reference colour, 123.3° anticlockwise from the right.
57	
58	Skin has a similar hue across complexions, and mostly differs in brightness and strength. If the trace from a face sits well to one side of the line, the picture has a cast.
59	
60	## Zoom in on a low-saturation picture
61	
62	The **1×**, **2×** and **4×** cells in the scope's bottom-right corner zoom in around the centre, to show small casts in a picture with little colour in it. Click a cell to choose it. The filled cell is the current zoom.
63	
64	Frame Job counts the pixels again at each zoom instead of enlarging the picture of the trace, so a magnified trace stays sharp.
65	
66	At 2× and 4×, a pixel too strong to fit on the square is left off, and it isn't piled up against the edge. At 1× everything fits.
67	
68	All six targets are too far out to fit at 2× and 4×. Each one becomes a 6 pt tick on the rim that points towards it, with its label inside the rim.
69	
70	Each slot keeps its own zoom when you pick another scope and come back, and when you hide the panel and show it again. A zoom lasts while the window is open. It isn't saved, and every slot starts at 1× in a new window. A cell works on the first click, even when its window isn't the active one.
71	
72	## Good to know
73	
74	- The scope measures the frame the preview composes, so it follows playback, your edits and [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/). It changes nothing in the project or in an export.
75	- The slot's caption says what the scope reads: "Rec. 709 · encoded", the picture's own encoded values.
76	- In an HDR (HLG) project the caption reads "Rec. 2100 HLG", and the targets and the skin line are redrawn for that colour space, with the skin line at 139.9°. With **Show SDR Version** on, the scope reads that SDR picture as it would in an SDR project. See [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/).
77	- The scope is a 224 pt square. If the preview area is too short for both slots, it shrinks with them and stays square. Under 360 pt tall, only the top slot shows.
78	
79	## With an agent
80	
81	`render_frame` measures a frame's vectorscope as numbers when an agent passes `vectorscope: true`, which is off by default. `vectorscope_zoom` chooses 1, 2 or 4, and is 1 unless set. The reply says what share of the frame is neutral and, at 2 and 4, what share lies off the plot. The counts, the targets and the skin line's angle go to a `.vectorscope.json` file beside the image. None of this changes a slot's zoom in the panel. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).
82	
83	## Related
84	
85	- [Scopes](/color/scopes/)
86	- [Waveform and RGB Parade](/color/waveform-and-parade/)
87	- [Histogram](/color/histogram/)
88	- [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/)
89	- [Brightness, contrast, saturation and hue](/color/color-section/)
90	- [Wheels](/color/wheels/)
91

1	---
2	title: "Waveform and RGB Parade"
3	description: "Read brightness and each colour channel across the frame, and find where highlights and shadows clip."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
8	
9	The Waveform shows how bright the picture is across the frame. The Parade shows the same thing for red, green and blue separately. Both tell you where the picture is clipping, which is hard to judge by eye.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu="View ▸ Scopes"
13	  keys="⌃⌘W"
14	  where="A slot's pop-up in the Scopes panel ▸ Waveform or Parade"
15	  tools="render_frame"
16	/>
17	
18	<Shot
19	  name="04b-preview-scopes.preview"
20	  alt="The Waveform in the top slot of the Scopes panel beside the preview: a dark panel labelled 0, 50 and 100 at its left, with a white trace, red marks along its top and bottom edges, and under it the readouts Highlights clipped 1.9 % and Shadows clipped 52.7 %."
21	/>
22	
23	To see them, press <kbd>⌃⌘W</kbd> to open the [Scopes](/color/scopes/) panel, then choose **Waveform** or **Parade** from a slot's pop-up. A new window's top slot is already on **Waveform**. Each takes 200 points of height when the pane has room, and [shrinks to fit](/color/scopes/#when-the-pane-is-short) when it doesn't.
24	
25	In an HDR project they read differently, and [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/) has the scale.
26	
27	## Read the waveform
28	
29	The Waveform plots the picture's luma (Y′, its brightness). Left to right in the scope is left to right across the frame, and height is brightness, with black at the bottom and white at the top. So a bright window on the left of the shot shows as a high patch on the left of the scope.
30	
31	Lines mark 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %, with 0, 50 and 100 labelled at the left. The trace is white on a near-black background in both light and dark appearance. The brighter a point in the trace, the more pixels sit there, on a log scale, so a level only a few pixels reach still shows.
32	
33	## Read the RGB parade
34	
35	The Parade shows red, green and blue as three waveforms side by side, in that order, each tinted its own colour. Each one works like the Waveform, with the same lines and the whole width of the frame.
36	
37	Use it to see a colour cast. Something that should be neutral grey sits at the same height in all three, and a channel sitting higher or lower is pulling the picture toward or away from that colour. **Temperature** and **Tint** in [Light](/color/light/), and the [wheels](/color/wheels/), are the usual ways to bring them back in line.
38	
39	## Find clipping
40	
41	A pixel clips high at the top level, where an 8-bit file would write 255, and low at the bottom level, where it would write 0. Detail at those levels has gone flat.
42	
43	**Clip marks** are red marks on the top and bottom edges of the scope. A mark sits over every column where at least 0.5 % of the pixels clip, on the top edge for highlights and the bottom edge for shadows, so you can see where in the frame it's happening. The Parade marks each channel on its own, so one channel can clip when the others don't.
44	
45	**Readouts** under the Waveform give the share of the whole frame, for example **Highlights clipped 1.8 %** and **Shadows clipped 52.7 %**. They show "—" until a frame has been measured. The [Histogram](/color/histogram/) has the same two readouts. The Parade and the Vectorscope have none.
46	
47	The readouts count everything in the frame. A black background around a smaller clip counts as clipped shadows, so a high figure may not be a problem with your footage. To bring highlights down, try **Exposure** or **Highlights** in [Light](/color/light/).
48	
49	## With an agent
50	
51	`render_frame` measures a frame's Waveform or Parade without the panel. Pass `waveform` or `parade` as true. Both are false by default. The tool's reply says what share of pixels clips high and low, and for the Parade it gives that for each channel, which the panel doesn't show as a number.
52	
53	A JSON file next to the image holds the raw counts, in 256 × 256 bins, with the clip marks and the clipping figures. It's named `<image path>.waveform.json` or `<image path>.parade.json`, and the Parade's holds red, green and blue separately. See [Tools: rendering and export](/mcp/tools-render-and-export/).
54	
55	## Related
56	
57	- [Scopes](/color/scopes/)
58	- [Vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/)
59	- [Histogram](/color/histogram/)
60	- [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/)
61	- [Light](/color/light/)
62

1	---
2	title: "Show Selection"
3	description: "See in grey exactly which pixels an adjustment clip's qualifier picks, so you can tune its ranges before you judge the grade."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	Show Selection replaces the preview with a grey picture of what a [qualifier](/color/qualifiers/) picks. It shows you which pixels an adjustment clip's grade reaches, so you can tune the ranges without guessing from the graded picture.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  menu="View ▸ Show Selection"
12	  where="Color tab ▸ Qualifier ▸ Show Selection"
13	  tools="render_frame"
14	  needs="An adjustment clip selected."
15	/>
16	
17	## Turn it on
18	
19	Select an [adjustment clip](/color/adjustment-clips/), then tick **Show Selection** in the **Qualifier** section of the [Color tab](/color/color-tab/), or choose **View ▸ Show Selection**. Do the same again to turn it off. It's off to begin with and has no keyboard shortcut. The **Qualifier** section only appears while every selected clip is an adjustment clip.
20	
21	The checkbox and the menu item are the same switch, and the menu item has a checkmark while it's on. The menu item is dimmed while Show Selection is off and no adjustment clip is selected.
22	
23	## Read the picture
24	
25	| The preview shows | What it means |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| White | The clip's grade applies in full here. |
28	| Black | The grade doesn't touch this pixel. |
29	| Grey | The grade applies in part, as it does across a range's soft edge. |

<system-reminder>
Contents of /Users/kevingalligan/devel/framejob/.claude/worktrees/help-docs/docs/site/CLAUDE.md:

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>
